beats.beat: Jory and Liora squeeze through the unmapped gap into a flooded back room.
Inside, they find a cluttered workbench of cracked glass vessels and corroded tools, not the furnishings of an ordinary household cellar.
Fresh-looking chisel marks scar the wall near a strongbox bolted to a support post, far too clean to be twenty years old.
The strongbox lock has no keyhole, only raised letters shaped like a name, faintly warm through Jory's glove despite the cold water.
Running low on air, they surface, debating who else could have cut those marks, and when.

turn.note: Maud's redirect toward hearing the whole letter sets up chapter 4's scene with Walter directly.

problems: "There was no keyhole. There was no slot, no hasp, no shackle." is a triple-plus list that reads as the rule-of-three tic rather than a deliberate accumulating period; trim to two items.

generic_prose.quote: Maud sat back on the thwart and looked at the water as if it owed her an explanation.
generic_prose.replace_with: ground it in a concrete action Maud actually takes with the chart or the boat, rather than a mood-simile about the water

trope_note: Serves the cursed object (lock's warmth, raised name) and what the old world knew (glass vessels, mortar) well; the map is wrong is carried over from ch2 rather than advanced here, which is fine since it isn't a beat for this chapter.
fixes: Trim 'There was no keyhole. There was no slot, no hasp, no shackle.' to two items so it doesn't read as a stock triple.
The chapter runs noticeably over target; cut redundancy in the warmth passage (the dog-simile sentence largely restates the line just before it) to tighten pacing.
Consider shortening the glass-vessel inventory ('Rows of it, racked and fallen...') by one clause — the mortar detail alone already does the work of signalling 'not a household cellar.'
